episodes.title: Killing of Joe Burnes
episodes.summary: The killing of Joe Burnes was the fatal shooting of a Black barber by a police officer in Kansas City, Missouri, reported in a wire dispatch dated January 2, 1882. Officer Lovett, who was said to have mistaken Burnes for a thief, shot him dead when he did not stop, and Lovett was reported exonerated. The item ran as a single paragraph of telegraph news in papers from Texas to Washington.

episodes.title: Assault on Ike Johnson
episodes.summary: The assault on Ike Johnson was a roadside attack on a Black man and his wife by two armed white men near the northern edge of Austin, Texas, on the night of January 2, 1882. When Officer J. L. Watts tried to arrest the two men at a house of ill fame later that night, one of them, Emmet McPhail, was shot dead and the other, Jeff Ake, wounded Watts. Papers outside Austin reported the episode as the killing of an ex-convict, and the attack on Johnson was described in detail mainly in the Austin Statesman's inquest coverage.

episodes.title: Hickory church burning
episodes.summary: The Hickory church burning was a night attack at Hickory, Mississippi, in which a Black church was fired into and burned and the town calaboose was burned, around the turn of 1881–82. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to the town to investigate. The one surviving report, from the Brandon Republican, described a community stirred by lawlessness that its officials had failed to stop.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Solomon
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Solomon took place at the Bossier parish jail in Bellevue, Louisiana, in the early hours of January 25, 1882, when ten or twelve unknown men took the jail keys from a deputy sheriff and hanged Solomon, a Black prisoner held on a charge of mule stealing. Hours earlier, by the deputy's account, Solomon had set his cell on fire in an attempt to escape. A coroner's jury found that he died by hanging at the hands of 'parties unknown,' and a Louisiana editor later held up the case as evidence that lynchers spared white criminals.

episodes.title: False report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey
episodes.summary: The false report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey was a January 1882 newspaper story that a mob in Randolph County, West Virginia, had hanged a Black man named Luckey after he shot the white father of the woman he had married. First printed by the Wheeling Register and copied by papers from Virginia to Dakota, the story was called a lie by the Randolph County press within a week. Papers that had carried it then retracted it as 'wholly untrue' or contradicted it.

episodes.title: Shooting of Dick Milner
episodes.summary: The shooting of Dick Milner took place in Hickman, Kentucky, probably on Monday, January 30, 1882, when City Marshal Barnes shot Milner, a Black man, in the leg as he ran from arrest. The wound was reported as not dangerous, and the only known account is a brief item in the local Hickman Courier.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Smith in San Antonio
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Smith in San Antonio took place on the morning of January 7, 1882, when Policeman Martinez shot a Black man named Smith in the hip while arresting him as a suspected robber. Smith survived with a flesh wound and was jailed. The case drew a local editorial in the San Antonio Evening Light that criticized arming the police and said Martinez faced a charge of assault with intent to murder.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas, was a reported threat by local citizens in January 1882 against Black men arrested for the murder and beheading of Jordan Thompson, a Black man. No lynching took place; Lewis pleaded guilty, was held in jail, and in April was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to twenty years. The threat is known only from a telegraphic brief, while the local paper described an excited crowd held back from the courthouse by guards.

episodes.title: Killing of Marshal Smith
episodes.summary: The killing of Marshal Smith was the fatal shooting of a Black preacher at his door on Carruthers' plantation at Clinton, Louisiana, on a Thursday night in late January 1882. Two white men, named in the dispatches as McKee and Singlebarre or Singlebury, were arrested for the murder on circumstantial evidence. The case reached the national press only as a brief wire item, and no later report of its outcome was found.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects (1882)
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects took place in January 1882 in Lincoln County, Georgia, where Black men jailed on an accusation of trying to burn the house of P. A. Cox near Lincolnton were threatened with lynching. County officials kept the prisoners from the threatened lynching, though an Augusta dispatch said fear for their lives persisted.

episodes.title: Beating of Jim Dunlap aboard the steamer James Lee
episodes.summary: The beating of Jim Dunlap aboard the steamer James Lee took place near Memphis, Tennessee, on the night of February 7, 1882, when the boat's crew attacked Dunlap, a Black deck passenger they accused of pushing the second mate overboard. He was beaten so badly that his life was despaired of before the boat's officers could reach him. The episode survives only as a short wire paragraph reprinted in small-town papers across several states.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Medley
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of William Medley took place in the Bear Quarter section of Norfolk County, Virginia, on about February 10, 1882, when residents tried to lynch a Black man accused of assaulting a five-year-old girl. Constable David Sykes got him to jail, and a Norfolk dispatch noted that the angry residents included both whites and Black people. Medley was later tried in the county court and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford took place on Sunday, February 12, 1882, when a crowd of about fifty went to the jail at Gainesville, Texas, intending to seize Alford, a Black music teacher accused of attempting to rape a fourteen-year-old girl. The crowd confined itself to talk and threats and withdrew when the jail guards refused it, and Alford remained in custody to await trial. The episode is known from a single item in the Waco Daily Examiner, which quoted the Gainesville Hesperian.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wm. Smeal
episodes.summary: The lynching of Wm. Smeal was the hanging of a Black farm worker by a mob near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road in Gwinnett County, Georgia, in mid-February 1882. Accused of stealing a horse, Smeal was taken from his cabin at night, whipped until he confessed, and hanged from a black-jack tree, where his body was found the next day. A short Athens dispatch carried the story nationally, and the local Jefferson Herald, while calling horse stealing a grave offense, condemned the killing as lynch law.

episodes.title: Nashville police shooting of a fleeing Black man (1882)
episodes.summary: The Nashville police shooting of a fleeing Black man took place in Nashville, Tennessee, on a Tuesday in mid-February 1882, apparently February 14, when a policeman fired at a man running from him. The bullet missed, and no one was hurt. The Memphis Daily Appeal noted the incident chiefly to remark that an officer who killed a fleeing person who was not a felon could be prosecuted for murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Redden
episodes.doubt: the local paper denied any attempt; Wilmington reports called sensational
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of James Redden was a reported effort by residents of the Odessa and Middletown area of New Castle County, Delaware, to lynch Redden, a Black man accused of raping a young girl, on 24–25 February 1882. Wilmington dispatches said officers resisted an organized attempt and took him safely to New Castle jail, but the local Middletown Transcript denied that any attempt was made. Redden was later tried, convicted of rape and hanged at New Castle on 25 August 1882.

episodes.title: Masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house
episodes.summary: The masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house was a night attack by four masked men on the home of a Black man near Cuthbert, Randolph County, Georgia, on Tuesday, 28 February 1882. Lawrence shot the first raider through the broken door, and the dead man was unmasked as Leonidas Bailey, a young white man of the county. A coroner's jury called the killing justifiable homicide, and the wire story of a Black householder killing a masked white raider ran in papers from Washington to Texas.

episodes.title: Centreville roadside ambush
episodes.summary: The Centreville roadside ambush was a shooting near Centreville, Texas, in February 1882, in which a white man named Lyle fired from hiding on two Black men named Hall and their wives as they rode in a wagon. Both men were killed and both women were reported mortally wounded. Carried by a St. Louis telegraph dispatch, the story ran in papers from West Virginia to California under headlines such as "Negroes Waylaid and Shot" and "Double Murder."

episodes.title: Watertown posse pursuit of a Black barber (1882)
episodes.summary: The Watertown posse pursuit of a Black barber was a manhunt in Watertown, apparently in Dakota Territory, reported in February 1882, in which a citizens' posse pursued an unnamed Black barber accused of attempting to rape a local woman. The single report said that he would be dealt with summarily if caught, but it gave no outcome, and no later report was found.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Taylor in the Maryland Penitentiary
episodes.summary: The killing of Robert Taylor took place on the afternoon of March 1, 1882, when James Byrne, an officer of the Maryland penitentiary in Baltimore, shot dead Taylor, a Black convict, in the prison foundry. A coroner's jury ruled the same day that Byrne had acted in self-defense, and the story ran in short wire items as the shooting of an insubordinate convict.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jack and Manuel Brown
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Jack and Manuel Brown was an unsuccessful attempt, on the night of March 1, 1882, at Lexington, Mississippi, to lynch two young Black men charged with attacking the storekeeper A. H. Pinkston. The attempt failed, and the only report of it was a single sentence in a Mississippi weekly's column of state news.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Sarver
episodes.summary: The lynching of Bob Sarver was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob near Franklin, Simpson County, Kentucky, on the night of Monday, March 6, 1882. Accused of attempting to rape a 16-year-old white girl, Sarver was taken from officers who were moving him by train and was hanged from a tree at the scene of the alleged attempt. A one-line Nashville dispatch carried the case to papers across the country, and three men were later reported arrested for the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French took place at Los Lunas, New Mexico, in early March 1882, when masked men took the three prisoners from the jail and hanged them from the nearest trees. The same mob took two Black prisoners from the jail, beat them and turned them loose. The story spread nationwide through an Albuquerque special to the Denver Republican, which presented the three hanged men as murderers.

episodes.title: Third Creek riot
episodes.summary: The Third Creek riot was a fight between whites and Black men at Third Creek station on the Western North Carolina Railroad on Saturday, March 11, 1882. About a hundred people took part, some with pistols and shotguns, and several Black men were badly but not fatally shot. A Salisbury militia company ended the fighting and jailed twenty-four rioters, and a Raleigh dispatch carried the story to papers across the country under headlines such as "Negroes Rioting in North Carolina."

episodes.title: Burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule
episodes.summary: The burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule was a pair of night-time attacks in March 1882 on the farm of Isham Edwards, a Black tenant on the Papy place, six miles from Tallahassee, Florida. Unidentified attackers burned about fifty panels of his fence on 11 March and the next night set his mule on fire in its stable, injuring the animal badly. The Weekly Floridian of Tallahassee condemned the attack on the mule as "fiendish cruelty," and the item was reprinted in Savannah.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Emma Johnson
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Emma Johnson took place at Summerfield, Georgia, about six miles from Macon, in March 1882, when a mob surrounded the officers holding Johnson, a young Black woman accused of killing a local merchant. The officers prevented the lynching and took her to Macon, where she was later convicted of murder in Bibb Superior Court. Papers across the country carried the story as a murder, with the mob mentioned in a single sentence.

episodes.title: Killing of Munroe Bloom
episodes.summary: The killing of Munroe Bloom was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a Georgia constable at Morrow's Station, on the Central railroad, in mid-March 1882. The constable had warrants charging Bloom and a second Black man with forgery, and Bloom, shot as he resisted arrest, was later found dead in the woods. A coroner's jury ruled the killing justifiable homicide, and the Atlanta dispatch reporting it ran in papers from Richmond and New York to Texas.

episodes.title: Assault on John H. Dorsey
episodes.summary: The assault on John H. Dorsey was an attack by a crowd on a Black man in Washington, D.C., on the afternoon of 17 March 1882. Three men named as members of the crowd were brought before the Police Court the next morning, where one was discharged and two were sentenced. The case drew only brief notices in two Washington evening papers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Edward Alberson and James Eato
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Edward Alberson and James Eato took place at the railroad depot in Roslyn, Long Island, New York, on the night of March 25, 1882, when a crowd threatened to lynch the two Black prisoners as officers removed them to the Queens County Jail. The officers got the men onto the train, and both later stood trial in Long Island City. The threat appears in a single New-York Tribune report on a robbery case that the paper followed closely.

episodes.title: Killing of escaped convicts near Big Springs, Texas (1882)
episodes.summary: The killing of escaped convicts near Big Springs, Texas, took place in March 1882, when rangers pursuing four Black convicts who had escaped from a Texas & Pacific Railroad work gang killed two of them and captured the other two. The convicts were said to have killed a guard in the escape, and the episode ran as a brief wire item in papers from Texas to West Virginia, Utah and California.

episodes.title: Killing of Elbert Rogers
episodes.summary: The killing of Elbert Rogers was the fatal shooting of a Black man accused of horse theft in Henderson County, Texas, in March 1882. Rogers was shot in the back while being pursued by a deputy sheriff and the horse's owner and died in the jail at Athens, and a coroner's jury attributed the shot to an unknown hand.

episodes.title: Sunflower Landing smallpox shooting
episodes.summary: The Sunflower Landing smallpox shooting was an attack on an unnamed Black man ill with smallpox, who was shot and whose cabin was burned at Sunflower Landing, Mississippi, as reported in March 1882. The only known account was a single line in a Kentucky paper's news column, which did not say who carried out the attack, when it happened, or whether the man survived.

episodes.title: Burning of Floyd King's house
episodes.summary: The burning of Floyd King's house was a suspected arson in early March 1882 in which the house of Floyd King, a Black man, was burned in Oconee, apparently Oconee County, Georgia. Two white tramps were thought to be responsible, but no arrest was reported, and the burning is known only from one short paragraph in the Savannah Morning News.

episodes.title: Arkadelphia road-work shooting
episodes.summary: The Arkadelphia road-work shooting was a shooting affray in early March 1882, six miles south of Arkadelphia, Arkansas, in which two white men, Joe Ross and Bud Henry, shot three Black men, Lewis Smith, Aaron Clark and Ed Clark. Smith was killed outright and a second man was reported unable to recover, though one later roundup said all three died. The two white men escaped, and the story ran as a brief wire item from Memphis to Minnesota and Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Killing of Bill Williams (Jim Titus)
episodes.summary: The killing of Bill Williams, also reported as Jim Titus, was the fatal shooting of a Black escaped convict by Memphis police sergeant James Scott at a cabin near Overton station, Tennessee, in mid-January 1882. The officers said he attacked them with an ax when they forced the door, and they left his body where it fell. The Memphis Daily Appeal told the story at length from the officers' side, while papers in Georgia, Texas, Missouri and Mississippi carried a one-sentence wire item.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph from Raleigh County, West Virginia
episodes.summary: The expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph was the beating and driving out of a Black schoolteacher by a mob in Raleigh County, West Virginia, reported in February 1882. According to Randolph's own statement, the mob beat him and ordered him to leave after a justice acquitted men he had had arrested, and he left to save his life. A Parkersburg paper headed its notice of the case "SHAMEFUL" while qualifying its comment on whether the statement was true.

episodes.title: Killing of James M. Davis
episodes.doubt: Beck-Tolnay lists James M. Davis (white) as lynched, Warren Co., Tenn., 1882-03-13. Our papers describe an ambush by moonshiners of a revenue officer; the month screen did not take it as a lynching. Inventory disagreement: code by our facts.
episodes.summary: The killing of James M. Davis was the ambush shooting of a deputy United States revenue collector by a concealed party of men described as moonshiners, on the Beersheba road about three miles from McMinnville, Warren County, Tennessee, on the afternoon of March 13, 1882. Davis, known as a 'celebrated raider of moonshiners,' was shot from his horse and finished with shots to the head, and the papers reported between twenty and more than thirty bullet wounds. The federal revenue service offered rewards for the killers, but no arrest appears in the coverage.
